newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish financial markets shrug off 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Irish financial markets shrug off 1997 budget.

text.p: Irish financial markets shrugged off the 1997 budget when they opened on Thursday, focusing instead on international developments, particularly a hefty overnight drop in sterling.
Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn announced "the biggest tax reduction package in the history of the State" in Wednesday's budget.
It was possibly the last to be held before an election which must take place by November this year.

He set out tax cuts and spending increases worth 650 million punts ($1.05 billion), including a reduction in the standard income tax rate to 26 percent from 27 percent, the first such cut in five years.
He also trimmed pay-related social insurance (PSRI), a payroll tax, by a percentage point and widened income tax bands.
Dealers said the budget, which had been well leaked and contained few surprises, prompted little market reaction.

Analysts welcomed Quinn's target for exchequer borrowing, which was slightly lower than many had expected at 637 million punts or 1.6 percent of GNP. But some said he had missed an opportunity to reduce Ireland's debt burden.
Quinn also set a target of 1.5 percent of GDP for the general goverment deficit, a move welcomed in the market.
His target is well below the three percent level set in the Maastricht treaty for European Economic and Monetary Union.
Economists agreed that Quinn's budget gave a fillip to an already booming economy but views were mixed on its consequences for Irish inflation.

"The budget is going to add to growth. It's clearly very expansionary and very pro-cyclical and that is not the ideal policy to have at the moment," Padhraic Garvey, economist at Riada Stockbrokers told Reuters.
But NCB Stockbrokers said it did not believe the budget would have any significant adverse inflationary or balance of payments consequences.

"The GDP/GNP growth rates we and the Department of Finance forecast are, we believe, within the underlying potential of an economy that is benefiting from significantly positive structural influences right now," economist Dermot O'Brien said.
Others said developments overseas were the real key to Irish inflation and interest rates as the budget.
"The main risk to inflation and interest rates in Ireland in the short term remains the outlook for sterling," John Beggs, economist at AIB Group Treasury, said.
Sterling proved the main focus for Irish markets on Thursday after a bruising overnight sell-off saw it shed nearly six pfennigs against the mark.
The Irish pound tracked it lower and had lost nearly two and a half pfennigs against the mark and close on one and a half cents against the dollar by 1040 GMT.
